title: About
text:
I built this project to get hands-on experience with Google BigQuery and BigQuery GIS, using a dataset I care about. My PhD research looks at wildfire smoke exposure and perinatal and infant health in British Columbia, so I wanted to understand the fire record behind the smoke.
The project covers a full, small-scale cloud data workflow:

extracting open government data in R
loading it into BigQuery
cleaning and checking it with SQL
running spatial queries with BigQuery GIS
querying BigQuery from R to build the charts and maps on this site

The Methods and SQL page documents every step, including the problems I ran into and how I handled them.
This is an independent portfolio project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the BC Wildfire Service or the Government of British Columbia.

Lightning versus people
Lightning and people start similar numbers of fires, but lightning fires account for most of the area burned. They tend to start in remote areas, where they can grow large before they are reached.

title: Fewer fires. Far more burned.
text:
Portfolio project · Google BigQuery · BigQuery GIS · R


75 years of BC Wildfire Service records, loaded into Google BigQuery and analysed with SQL and BigQuery GIS. The number of fires each season hasn’t gone up, but the area they burn has.
Explore the data How it was built Code on GitHub
Banner: one stripe per fire season, 1950 to 2025. Brighter stripes mean more area burned.

title: Fewer fires. Far more burned.
text:
Where the largest fires burned
Every fire of 10,000 hectares or more from 1950 to 2025 (255 fires), coloured by decade. Click a fire for its details, or use the layer menu (top right) to show or hide decades. Dashed circles mark 50 km around five communities used in the spatial analysis.

title: Fewer fires. Far more burned.
text:
What the data show

Area burned has risen sharply while the number of fires has not. Annual fire counts since 2020 are within or below the historical range, but the average area burned each year is many times higher than in earlier decades.
2023 was an extreme outlier. About 3.86M hectares burned, nearly three times the next largest seasons, 2018 and 2017.
Lightning drives most of the area burned. Lightning caused about half of all fires but 77% of area burned.
Area burned is concentrated in the north. The Prince George Fire Centre accounts for over half of all area burned since 1950.
Area burned near communities has increased. Within 50 km of Kamloops, more land burned from 2020 to 2025 than in any earlier decade.


This is an independent portfolio project using open BC Wildfire Service data. It is not an official BC Wildfire Service product, and it is not intended for legal, planning, or insurance decisions. See Methods and SQL for data sources, cleaning steps, and limitations.

title: Methods and SQL
text:
1. Extract (R) Downloaded two BC Data Catalogue layers with bcdata, one fire season at a time.


2. Prepare (R) Harmonised column types, repaired and simplified shapes, and exported CSVs with geometry as WKT text.


3. Load (BigQuery) Uploaded both files to a BigQuery sandbox dataset, with an explicit schema for the incidents.


4. Transform and check (SQL) Built GEOGRAPHY columns, cleaned dates, and ran data quality checks.


5. Analyse and share (SQL, R) Summarised by year, fire centre, and cause, ran a spatial query, and pulled the results into R with bigrquery.


All the code is in the GitHub repository: R scripts in R/ and SQL in sql/.

Data



Dataset
What it contains
Records




BC Wildfire Fire Incident Locations - Historical
One point per incident tracked by BC Wildfire Service, with year, cause, fire centre, and dates
200,479


BC Wildfire Fire Perimeters - Historical
Mapped fire perimeter polygons, with size in hectares
24,751



Both datasets are published by the Government of British Columbia (BC Wildfire Service) through the BC Data Catalogue, and were accessed in November 2026. They are not intended for legal purposes.

title: Methods and SQL
section: Problems found, and how they were handled
text:
Problems found, and how they were handled

Large downloads failed. Requesting all 200,479 incidents at once failed partway through, so the download was split into one request per fire season, with automatic retries.
Column types changed between years. For example, VERSION_NUMBER is text in some years and a number in others. Mixed columns were converted to text before combining.
Impossible dates. BigQuery rejected three rows on load because of ignition dates with years such as 223 and 915. The incidents were reloaded with dates as text, then parsed in SQL with SAFE.PARSE_DATE. In total, five dates before 1900 were set to missing. Annual summaries use FIRE_YEAR, so they are not affected.
Non-fire incidents. Only 156,624 of the 200,479 incidents are true fires. The rest are nuisance fires, smoke chases, duplicates, and other incident types. Fire counts use FIRE_TYPE = 'Fire' only.

title: Methods and SQL
text:
Data quality checks

Geometry: all 200,479 points and 24,751 perimeters produced valid BigQuery geographies.
Area: for the largest fires, area calculated from the polygons with ST_AREA was within about 0.5% of the recorded size. That is consistent with simplifying the shapes to 50 m.
Fire centre: derived from the first letter of the fire number, and cross-checked against the FIRE_CENTRE code. Each letter matched exactly one code for all 156,624 fires.

title: Methods and SQL
text:
Key SQL

Building geography columns
-- Points: build a geography from longitude and latitude
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE `bc-wildfire-bigquery.bc_wildfire.incidents` AS
SELECT
  * EXCEPT (IGNITION_DATE, FIRE_OUT_DATE),
  IF(SAFE.PARSE_DATE('%Y-%m-%d', IGNITION_DATE) >= DATE '1900-01-01',
     SAFE.PARSE_DATE('%Y-%m-%d', IGNITION_DATE), NULL) AS IGNITION_DATE,
  IF(SAFE.PARSE_DATE('%Y-%m-%d', FIRE_OUT_DATE) >= DATE '1900-01-01',
     SAFE.PARSE_DATE('%Y-%m-%d', FIRE_OUT_DATE), NULL) AS FIRE_OUT_DATE,
  ST_GEOGPOINT(LONGITUDE, LATITUDE) AS geog
FROM `bc-wildfire-bigquery.bc_wildfire.fire_incidents_raw`;

-- Polygons: parse WKT text, repairing minor geometry problems
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE `bc-wildfire-bigquery.bc_wildfire.perimeters` AS
SELECT
  * EXCEPT (geometry_wkt),
  SAFE.ST_GEOGFROMTEXT(geometry_wkt, make_valid => TRUE) AS geog
FROM `bc-wildfire-bigquery.bc_wildfire.fire_perimeters_raw`;


Area burned within 50 km of communities
-- ST_DWITHIN finds perimeters within 50 km; ST_INTERSECTION clips each
-- perimeter to a 50 km buffer so only the nearby burned area is counted.
WITH communities AS (
  SELECT name, ST_GEOGPOINT(lon, lat) AS pt
  FROM UNNEST([
    STRUCT('Kamloops' AS name, -120.327 AS lon, 50.675 AS lat),
    ('Kelowna', -119.496, 49.888),
    ('Prince George', -122.749, 53.917),
    ('Williams Lake', -122.141, 52.141),
    ('Fort St. John', -120.846, 56.252)
  ])
)
SELECT
  c.name AS community,
  DIV(p.FIRE_YEAR, 10) * 10 AS decade,
  COUNT(*) AS n_fires_within_50km,
  SUM(ST_AREA(ST_INTERSECTION(p.geog, ST_BUFFER(c.pt, 50000)))) / 10000
    AS area_burned_within_50km_ha
FROM communities AS c
JOIN `bc-wildfire-bigquery.bc_wildfire.perimeters` AS p
  ON ST_DWITHIN(p.geog, c.pt, 50000)
WHERE p.FIRE_YEAR BETWEEN 1950 AND 2025
GROUP BY community, decade
ORDER BY community, decade;


Preparing shapes for the web map
-- One row per large fire, with shapes simplified to 250 m in BigQuery
-- so the web map stays fast
SELECT
  p.FIRE_YEAR, p.FIRE_NUMBER, i.INCIDENT_NAME, p.FIRE_SIZE_HECTARES,
  ST_ASTEXT(ST_SIMPLIFY(p.geog, 250)) AS wkt
FROM `bc-wildfire-bigquery.bc_wildfire.perimeters` AS p
LEFT JOIN `bc-wildfire-bigquery.bc_wildfire.incidents` AS i
  ON i.FIRE_NUMBER = p.FIRE_NUMBER
 AND i.FIRE_YEAR = p.FIRE_YEAR
 AND i.FIRE_TYPE = 'Fire'
WHERE p.FIRE_SIZE_HECTARES >= 10000
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
  PARTITION BY p.FIRE_NUMBER, p.FIRE_YEAR ORDER BY i.IGNITION_DATE
) = 1;
The full set of queries is in sql/. Each analysis query processed between about 14 and 31 MB, well within the BigQuery sandbox’s free monthly allowance.

title: Methods and SQL
section: Why the results are saved as files
text:
Why the results are saved as files
BigQuery sandbox tables expire after 60 days. The analysis was run once in BigQuery, and the results were saved to the repository (R/03_export_results.R), so this site keeps working after the cloud tables expire. The full pipeline can be rerun from the scripts.

title: Methods and SQL
text:
Limitations

Perimeter mapping has changed over time. Before about 2006, few small fires were mapped, so fire counts come from incident points. Area totals are dominated by large fires, which were mapped throughout, but early totals may be slightly underestimated.
Holdover fires. Some fires overwinter and are recorded again the next season under a new number, so some area may be counted in more than one season.
Reburns. Area that burned more than once is counted each time, including in the 50 km community totals.
Simplified shapes. Perimeters were simplified to 50 m for analysis and 250 m for the map. That is fine for provincial summaries, but not for property-level work.
Descriptive only. No adjustment is made for changes in detection, suppression policy, reporting, or climate.
